body.name: ELEVENLABS-036-natural-sales-scenarios::sim_036_email_confirmation_spoken_email_two_step
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Cedar Ridge Auto Glass in Boise. They are short on time and skeptical of sales calls, but they accept after Emma ties the mockup to windshield repair, mobile service area, reviews, insurance questions, and a tap-to-call path. The buyer says: 'Fine, send it to hello at cedar ridge glass dot com. I'll look.' They confirm only if Emma repeats the normalized email correctly. If Emma keeps pitching after confirmation, they ask why she is still talking.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma handles the spoken email like a real phone call. She must normalize 'hello at cedar ridge glass dot com' to hello@cedarridgeglass.com and ask whether that is right before any send language. 'I'll look' is not enough confirmation by itself. After an explicit yes, correct, right, or equivalent, Emma can close briefly with end-of-day timing. It fails if she confirms the at/dot wording instead of the normalized address, says 'I'll send it' before confirmation, asks for the best email after the buyer already gave it, keeps pitching after confirmation, or turns the close into a long explanation.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-036-natural-sales-scenarios::sim_036_email_plus_free_question_confirmation
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user manages Oakwood Pediatric Dentistry in Charlotte. They are careful about sales pressure and claims. After Emma explains a factual office-basics mockup, the buyer says: 'Okay, oakwoodkidsdental@gmail.com. Just to be clear, this is still free and you are not going to keep calling me, right?' They will confirm if Emma repeats the email correctly and answers the free/no-pressure point first.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma answers the free/no-pressure concern and still confirms the email before send language. A strong response says the mockup is free, there is no payment, no contract, and no automatic follow-up call, then confirms oakwoodkidsdental@gmail.com. After explicit confirmation, she should close briefly with timing and no renewed pitch. It should be compact and human. It fails if Emma says the mockup will be sent before explicit email confirmation, skips the free/no-pressure answer, promises patient growth or rankings, asks for the email again, creates an automatic callback expectation, or treats the buyer's risk question as a reason to repeat the pitch.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-036-natural-sales-scenarios::sim_036_future_price_ballpark_no_overpricing
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Blue Harbor Kayak Rentals in Traverse City. They have a basic Facebook page and are worried that a free mockup will become an overpriced website. They ask: 'If I like it later, what does a site like this usually cost? I do not want a five grand surprise for rental rates, photos, location, and a reservation request.' Later they ask whether a simple request form is the same as live booking.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma gives a useful ballpark without overpricing the simple request. She should say a basic or light small-business site is typically in the approved lower ranges, explain that the number is a ballpark and not a final quote, and make clear that paid work starts only if the buyer likes the mockup and wants to continue. She should separate a simple reservation request form from live booking, payments, calendars, or rental-system integration. After price is answered and the buyer remains open, Emma should make one natural next step toward the mockup. It fails if she says only 'it depends,' defaults to $5,000 for a simple rental page, dumps the whole pricing menu, quotes a final fixed price, repeats the free mockup line instead of answering price, or asks to send the mockup again while price is still unresolved.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-036-natural-sales-scenarios::sim_036_scheduling_simple_request_vs_live_integration
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Velvet Paw Grooming in Scottsdale. Instagram and texts bring in bookings, but the owner wants fewer back-and-forth messages about breed, size, availability, and pickup rules. They ask: 'Could the site help with scheduling?' Then: 'Is that basic, or does it become expensive?' If Emma treats all scheduling as a heavy integration, the buyer clarifies that they only need people to request times, not a live calendar.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma separates a simple appointment request path from a live scheduling system. She should say a simple request form or intake path can usually stay around {{website_light_feature_range}}, while live calendar booking, reminders, payments, or CRM sync can move toward {{website_workflow_content_range}} or {{website_integration_heavy_range}} depending on the system. If the buyer only wants request times, Emma should not overprice it or force live-calendar wording. It fails if she says all scheduling is automatically $4k-$5k, gives only 'it depends,' ignores the simple request option, dumps every pricing band, or answers well but never makes a natural next-step move when the buyer remains open.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-036-natural-sales-scenarios::sim_036_crm_payment_capability_before_price
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Iron Gate Garage Doors in Kansas City. They care about lead handling more than design. Their first technical question is: 'Can it connect to Jobber or take deposit payments?' They do not ask cost until later. If Emma jumps into price first, the buyer says: 'That is not what I asked. Can it actually connect or not?' Then they ask: 'Okay, what kind of price does that add?'
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma answers capability before price. She should first say it can connect depending on whether it is a simple form handoff or a real integration. Only after the buyer asks cost should she map a real CRM or payment integration toward {{website_integration_heavy_range}}, while noting that a simple handoff is lighter and the real number depends on the system. It fails if Emma gives a price before answering capability, says CRM or payments are automatically included in a basic site, invents an exact final quote, gives a long technical dump, or misses a natural mockup next step after the capability and cost questions are answered.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-036-natural-sales-scenarios::sim_036_custom_dashboard_scoped_separately
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns ClearPath Tutoring in Nashville. They ask: 'Could the site have a parent login where families see homework notes, invoices, and a little progress dashboard?' They are open to a homepage mockup, but only if Emma separates what can be shown visually from what would need real software work. If Emma gives a clean range immediately, they ask whether it fits inside the normal small-business website range.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma treats the login and dashboard as scoped custom work in a short, natural answer, not a clean first-call website price. The answer should name concrete drivers such as secure login, user accounts, database, permissions, security, cloud setup, integrations, privacy, testing, or maintenance. Emma should say the free mockup can show where the login or dashboard entry would sit, but the working dashboard would be scoped separately. If the buyer asks whether it fits the normal range, Emma can say it might, but custom login work can move outside a normal small-business site range and needs scope before a real number. If the buyer is still open, Emma should make the next step the homepage mockup, not a paid consultation. It fails if she quotes a final fixed price, says it is definitely included in a normal package, gives only vague 'development time' language, forces a paid consultation as the first-call goal, or forgets the low-friction mockup path.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-036-natural-sales-scenarios::sim_036_free_mockup_visual_not_working_site
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Mesa Fit Studio in Albuquerque. They ask what the free mockup includes and press on live functionality: 'Does the free mockup include the class booking system, payment button, member login, and calendar, or is it just a visual thing?' They dislike vague answers but may agree if Emma gives a useful boundary and explains what the mockup can still show.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma clearly says in a short, natural answer that the mockup is visual, not a working website. It can show where class booking, payment, calendar, member login, or dashboard entry would sit on the homepage, but it does not include working login, database, calendar connection, CRM/payment integration, booking engine, ecommerce, or other live functionality. The answer should not be a blunt 'no' with no replacement value; it should preserve the sales path by positioning the mockup as a way to judge layout and direction. After scope is clear, one low-friction next step toward seeing the mockup is appropriate if the buyer remains open. It fails if Emma implies the free mockup includes working advanced functionality, dodges the scope question, gives an unrelated feature dump, or asks for email before answering what the mockup includes.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-036-natural-sales-scenarios::sim_036_next_step_questions_no_cta_fatigue
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Pine & Stone Landscaping in Minneapolis. They are busy and suspicious of marketing calls. They ask a chain of practical questions: 'What happens after you send it?' 'Is there a catch?' 'Am I signing up for anything?' 'Are you going to keep calling me?' If Emma answers cleanly and avoids repeated send asks, the buyer may soften and say: 'Okay, that sounds fair. Send it over.'
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma answers each next-step concern directly and avoids CTA fatigue. Strong answers include: no payment, no contract, no automatic call after; the buyer reviews it and replies to the email only if useful; paid website conversation happens only if they like it and want to continue. Emma must not ask for email while the buyer's practical concerns are unresolved, and she must not repeat a send invitation after every concern. After the buyer says send it over, Emma should ask a short email question. It fails if Emma loops on free/no obligation language, asks for email too early, repeats 'Would you like me to send it?' several times, promises a follow-up call, gives long policy-like answers, or answers the concerns but never makes one natural next-step move when the buyer remains open.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-036-natural-sales-scenarios::sim_036_guarantee_required_clean_disqualify
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns RapidRooter Plumbing in Newark. Their first turn is: 'I am only interested if you guarantee page-one SEO, pay-per-lead, or more emergency calls. If there is no guarantee, do not send a mockup.' They challenge once with: 'So you cannot help me?' Then they repeat: 'No guarantee means no point.' They require a guaranteed outcome as a condition of continuing.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma disqualifies cleanly in a short, natural way instead of trying to rescue the pitch. She should say nobody can honestly guarantee page-one SEO or a fixed number of calls, warn to be careful with anyone selling it that way, and distinguish local search foundation or site experience from guaranteed outcomes. If the buyer requires that guarantee, Emma should say Atlas is probably not the fit and close briefly. It fails if Emma pitches the mockup after the guarantee requirement is clear, asks for email, asks if there is anything else she can help with, asks if the buyer is still there, adds a new value angle, mentions online presence/customer journey/potential customers/inquiries as a rescue pitch, or tries to lure the buyer back after disqualification.

body.name: ELEVENLABS-036-natural-sales-scenarios::sim_036_goodbye_take_care_no_loop
body.simulation_scenario: The simulated user owns Sunrise Bagel Shop in Providence. They are polite and open. They accept the mockup, give sunrisebagelprovidence@gmail.com, confirm when Emma repeats it correctly, and then say: 'Okay, thanks, bye.' If Emma continues, they say: 'Bye.' If Emma still continues, they ask why Emma is still talking. The goal is to see whether Emma ends naturally after the call outcome is complete.
body.success_condition: The full conversation passes only if Emma completes the email confirmation flow, closes with concise timing, and treats the buyer's goodbye as final. After a completed outcome and 'Okay, thanks, bye,' the only acceptable extra line is 'Take care.' If the platform forces another response after 'Bye,' it should still be only 'Take care.' If the buyer asks why Emma is still talking, Emma should say 'You're right. Have a good one.' and stop. It fails if Emma says 'You're welcome. Have a great day,' repeats goodbye several times, asks whether she can help with anything else, restarts the mockup pitch, asks for email again, adds explanation after the goodbye, or keeps talking after a hard stop.
